oneLiner: An integrated major whose 2026 earnings are being set by the Middle East supply shock. The market is betting that Brent stays above $80 after the conflict and that Hess, Tengiz and Venezuela growth turn the windfall into a higher earnings base rather than a peak.

verdict.summary: Chevron is executing well: low-cost barrels, a near-halved net debt load and steady buybacks. But the price already capitalises a mid-$80s Brent 2027, the level at which forward EPS of roughly $15-16 works. Our base case of $80 Brent and normal-but-firm refining is worth somewhat less than that. The ~$9 a share of dividends due by end-2027 roughly closes the gap, so the skew is flat, not attractive. Two things would move the view. If Hormuz constraints run into H2 2027 and the EIA lifts its 2027 Brent above $90, we turn positive. If the 2027 budget in December breaks $20B organic or buybacks drop below $2.5B a quarter, we turn cautious.
wtb: Brent averages at least ~$80 in 2027 (EIA October STEO: $84) - roughly where FY2027 EPS reaches $13-14.
The 2027 organic capex budget (due December 2026) stays within the $18-19B 2026 range despite higher exploration, Venezuela and Project Kilby.
Buybacks hold at $2.5-3B a quarter, taking shares outstanding below ~1.90B by end-2027 (1.951B at Sep 30, 2026).
Production returns to YoY growth by Q2 2027 as Uaru and Venezuela ramp; Q3 2026 was below Q3 2025.

bear.why: Hormuz flows normalise in H1 2027 and OPEC+ chases share: Brent averages ~$62 and refining cracks fall back to mid-cycle. Net margin ~7.6% (above FY2025's 6.7% on cost cuts, a full year of Hess and TCO at full rate). Buybacks drop to the bottom of the range, so diluted shares are ~1.92B. The market pays a trough multiple on trough EPS, as it did on FY2025 (a ~4.8% dividend yield floor).

base.why: Brent averages ~$80 as Middle East output recovers slowly (EIA sees regional shut-ins persisting into 2027); cracks stay above mid-cycle. Net margin ~11.5% and ~1.90B diluted shares on $10-12B of buybacks. The market pays a mid-cycle multiple because 2028 looks similar, not higher.

bull.why: Supply stays constrained through 2027: Brent averages ~$95 and product markets stay tight. Net margin ~13% on 2026-like refining, and buybacks lift toward $3B+ a quarter for ~1.88B diluted shares. The multiple compresses because the market treats these as peak earnings.

scenarioModel.note: EPS = revenue x net margin / diluted shares: bear $175B x 7.6% / 1.92B = $6.93; base $225B x 11.5% / 1.90B = $13.62; bull $265B x 13.0% / 1.88B = $18.32. Revenue maps to the oil deck from history: FY2025 $184B at ~$69 Brent; FY2026 ~$250B at ~$96 (9M $180.0B plus a ~$70B Q4 estimate). Multiples run inverse to the cycle and are applied to FY2027 EPS at end-2027. Values exclude ~$9/share of dividends paid between now and end-2027 at $1.78 a quarter. All inputs are Siberforge estimates, not consensus.

debates.q: What oil price is the stock discounting, and does it outlast the conflict?
debates.bull: EIA's October STEO raised 2027 Brent to $84 (from $74) and assumes Middle East flows stay constrained through Q4 2026, with East-West pipeline attacks keeping physical markets tight. At that deck, forward EPS in the mid-teens is achievable.
debates.bear: The reverse DCF needs TTM FCF to grow ~4.4% a year for a decade, yet revenue fell ~7.9% a year over FY2022-2025 as prices normalised. Pre-spike forecasts (EIA August: $69 for 2027; Morgan Stanley $75 for end-2026) show where the deck goes once Hormuz reopens.
debates.view: The stock is priced for the bull side of this debate, not the base. We do not pay for a war premium in 2027 earnings. The multiple lands between 14x and 21x depending on the answer, but EPS swings far more than the multiple, so the deck dominates.

signpost.metric: EIA STEO 2027 Brent forecast and the Dec-2027 Brent future
signpost.threshold: bullish if above $90; bearish if below $72

debates.q: Is rising capex buying growth, or just holding production flat?
debates.bull: 2026 spending tracks the low end of its range while Permian unit costs keep falling (thesis 1). The new spend is cheap per barrel: Venezuela is self-funding, and infrastructure-led exploration has a 40% success rate (15 discoveries in two years).
debates.bear: TTM capex is 8.8% of revenue vs 5.1% in 2022. Q3 2026 production of 3,980 MBOED was below Q3 2025's 4,086 (entitlement effects, Middle East disruption). 2027 adds a larger exploration program, Venezuela and Kilby power on top.
debates.view: The Q3 volume dip is mostly price-driven entitlement loss, not decline, so it does not break the case. But the December budget is the discipline test. Capex creep at high prices is how majors destroyed value in 2011-2014.

signpost.metric: 2027 organic capex budget and 2027 production growth guide
signpost.threshold: bearish if organic capex above $20B or growth guide below 2%

debates.q: Will buybacks retire the Hess shares, or do they get cut in the next downturn?
debates.bull: With leverage at a cycle low, management reiterated $2.5-3B a quarter and no change to the capital-allocation framework despite Q3 price volatility. The shares outstanding count is already falling.
debates.bear: The all-stock Hess deal lifted the diluted count ~14.5% YoY (Q2 2026 vs Q2 2025), and at $10-12B a year it takes about five years to buy back. In 2020 repurchases were the first lever cut.
debates.view: The buyback is the swing factor in per-share growth: in the base case it adds ~3% a year to EPS. Holding the pace through a sub-$70 quarter would prove the post-Hess model works. A cut would put the bear multiple in play.

signpost.threshold: below $2.5B in any quarter with Brent above $70 = bearish

catalysts: Nov 2026 and monthly: EIA STEO 2027 Brent path and Middle East shut-in estimates (debate 1).
Early Dec 2026 (date unverified): 2027 capex budget and production outlook (debate 2).
Dec 10, 2026: $1.78 quarterly dividend paid; end-Q4 2026: Bakken midstream deconsolidation closes with a $3-4B non-cash after-tax special loss.
Q4 2026 - Q2 2027: Uaru (Stabroek, ~250 kbd gross) first oil, plus Venezuela at ~300 kbd gross by year-end 2026 (debate 2).
Late Jan 2027: Q4 2026 results - buyback pace and the end-2026 $3-4B structural cost-reduction target (debate 3).
Late 2026 (expected): Project Kilby FID; TCO concession-extension talks (no timeline given).
thesis: Low-cost barrels carry the base. The Permian has held above 1 MMBOED for six quarters. Capex per barrel is down 25%+, drilling and completion spend -40% and facilities -50%. TCO runs above 1 MMbpd gross after a 20% expansion and is framed at ~$6B of FCF at $70 Brent (company figure via Hudson Labs, unverified).

The windfall went to the balance sheet first. Total debt fell from $40.8B at year-end 2025 to $33.5B at Sep 30, 2026, and net debt from $34.5B to $20.7B (net debt ratio 9.6%). A $60s year can now be absorbed without cutting the dividend.

Downstream is the hedge that worked. U.S. downstream earned $3.6B in Q3 2026 vs $638M a year earlier, with crude units at 98% utilization and distillate yield at 46%. Refining offset weaker upstream realizations.

Cheap long-dated options. Venezuela targets ~600 kbd gross by 2031 at under $20/bbl all-in and self-funding, per management. Project Kilby has a 20-year Microsoft PPA for 2.67 GW with first power in 2028. Neither is in a mid-cycle multiple.
risks: Oil normalisation sets the value. Pricing in 2026 is a supply shock, not demand: the EIA's 2025 Brent average was $69. A reopened Hormuz takes FY2027 EPS toward the bear case, and the stock has the dividend floor but little else.

Reported earnings are noisy. Q3 carried -$1.58B of timing effects and -$294M of special items. Adjusted FCF included a $1B TCO loan repayment and asset-sale proceeds, and Q4 will book a $3-4B non-cash Bakken midstream loss. Higher prices also shrink entitlement barrels.
Kazakhstan concentration. TCO is now a large cash generator that exports almost entirely via the CPC pipeline through Russia. Its concession expires in 2033, and extension talks have no timeline.
Non-operated and political growth. Guyana pace and the Uaru start-up are set by ExxonMobil as operator (Chevron 30%). Venezuela growth depends on a US policy stance that can reverse.

Capex creep at high prices. New exploration, Venezuela and power projects all arrive while cash is abundant. If the 2027 budget resets above the 2026 range, FCF lags earnings exactly when the deck turns (debate 2).

latestQuarter.label: Q3 2026 (ended Sep 30, 2026; reported Oct 30, 2026)
points: Earnings $9.9B, diluted EPS $5.06; adjusted $10.4B ($5.28) vs ~$4.83 consensus (21 analysts); adjusted earnings $1.6B below Q2 on lower upstream realizations, liftings and timing.
Sales and other operating revenues $65.2B (vs ~$61.6B expected); upstream earnings $5.7B, downstream $4.9B; ROCE 17.7%.
Production 3,980 MBOED (Q3 2025: 4,086); U.S. 2,043, international 1,937; record natural gas above 9 Bcf/d.
CFFO $16.0B ($16.6B ex working capital); capex $4.0B; FCF $12.0B, adjusted FCF $14.2B.
Dividends $3.5B plus buybacks $2.5B; total debt cut $3.5B in the quarter; net debt / CFFO 0.4x.

latestProse: Q3 2026 (reported Oct 30) beat on adjusted EPS but was a weaker upstream quarter than Q2. Brent swung between about $68 and $132 intra-quarter (CFO), averaging $114 in September (EIA). Lower realizations, lower liftings and unfavorable timing effects took adjusted earnings $1.6B below Q2, while downstream rose on refining margins and record U.S. crude throughput. Volumes dipped YoY on production-sharing entitlement effects and Middle East disruption, even as the Gulf of America set a deepwater record and Venezuela entered equity accounting with one month of production. Cash was stronger than earnings: higher TCO distributions plus a $1B TCO loan repayment, partly offset by a working-capital build from the late-quarter price jump that management expects to reverse.
guidanceProse: Chevron gives no EPS guidance. 2026 organic capex is tracking the low end of $18-19B, with spending stepping up in Q4. 2026 production growth was guided at 7-10% (per the Hudson Labs preview, unverified against the company deck); the year-to-date average is 3,970 MBOED. Management reiterated buybacks at $2.5-3B a quarter and the $1.78 quarterly dividend, its 39th consecutive year of increases. The $3B structural cost-reduction run-rate is in place against a $3-4B end-2026 target, and Bakken midstream tariffs fall ~50% under the new agreements. Deconsolidating $3.7B of midstream debt adds ~0.5pt to ROCE. 2027 detail comes with the December budget; so far the only commitment is exploration spend ~50% above the 2025 baseline (~20 wells a year), with Bakken rigs going from three to two while holding ~180 kboe/d.
segments: Upstream (Q3 2026 earnings $5.7B: U.S. $3.3B, international $2.4B): Permian, DJ, Bakken, Gulf of America; Tengiz (TCO), Guyana (30% of Stabroek), Australian LNG (Gorgon/Wheatstone above nameplate), Eastern Mediterranean gas, Venezuela (equity-accounted from Q3 2026).
Downstream (Q3 2026 earnings $4.9B: U.S. $3.6B, international $1.3B): refining, marketing, chemicals (CPChem); Pascagoula +7% capacity by 2030 and Pasadena ~15% debottleneck planned.
All Other (Q3 2026 -$0.7B): corporate, financing, and new energies including Project Kilby power.
competitive: ExxonMobil (XOM): operates Stabroek with 45%, so Chevron's Guyana growth rides Exxon's schedule. It is the larger integrated peer on refining and chemicals.
ConocoPhillips (COP): the pure-play E&P comparator on shale efficiency and FCF yield, with no downstream offset when crude and cracks diverge.
Shell and BP: European majors at persistent valuation discounts; Chevron's U.S. listing, Guyana stake and dividend record support its premium.
OPEC+ spare capacity and Middle East export routes are the real competitor: how fast Hormuz-constrained barrels return decides the 2027 deck.
moat: Scale, integration and a reloaded resource base. A 30% stake in Stabroek, an expanded Tengiz and advantaged Permian acreage give decades of low-breakeven barrels, and U.S. refining captures product tightness when upstream realizations lag. Low leverage and 39 years of dividend increases let Chevron buy back stock and invest countercyclically when leveraged rivals retreat.

valPresets.note: Calibrate off normalized FCF (roughly mid-$20s billions at $75-85 Brent with Hess and TCO at full run-rate), not 2026's war-premium quarters. Bear's negative growth is an oil-price path ($60s Brent), not operational failure; bull layers 2-3% volume growth on a $90+ deck. Fade to a 2.5% terminal - generous for a hydrocarbon business, which is the honest tension in the model.

changelog.change: Rebuilt to v3 after the Q3 2026 print (adjusted EPS $5.28 vs ~$4.83 consensus, FCF $12.0B, net debt $20.7B). The view moved from implicitly constructive to Neutral: the stock now prices a mid-$80s 2027 Brent, above our $80 base.
